subject: se
question: Explain testing. Explain integration testing.
title: Testing, From Zero
answer: Testing = executing software with the intent of finding errors before users do.
Integration testing checks the interfaces between modules that each pass unit testing.
Big bang: all modules combined at once.
Top-down: start from the main module; missing lower modules replaced by STUBS.
Bottom-up: start from the lowest modules; a DRIVER simulates the calling module.
Stub fakes the bottom, driver fakes the top.

subject: se
question: Draw and explain a UML Sequence Diagram for a Library Management System showing the process of issuing a book (Student, Librarian, Library Management System).
title: Chat Between Three
answer: A sequence diagram shows how objects interact, in time order.
Three lifelines (dashed vertical lines): Student, Librarian, LMS (Library Management System).
Six messages top to bottom: requestBook(), isAvailable(), available (reply), issueBook(), confirm(dueDate) (reply), hands over book (reply).
Solid arrow = call/request, dashed arrow = reply.
Memory trick: the lifeline is the clock, the arrows are the words.

subject: se
question: Name any three UML diagrams used to represent the behavioural view of a system. Briefly explain the purpose of each.
title: Floor Plan vs Life
answer: Behavioural diagrams show what the system DOES (structural diagrams show what it is made of).
Use case diagram: actors and the functions (use cases) they use. Purpose: capture what users want from the system.
Sequence diagram: messages between objects in time order. Purpose: show how objects collaborate in one scenario.
Activity diagram: a flowchart of steps, decisions, start and end. Purpose: model the workflow step by step.
Memory trick: use case = WHO, sequence = WHEN, activity = HOW.

subject: se
question: Draw a UML Class Diagram for a Library Management System using the classes Student, Book, Librarian, Issue Record and Fine, with attributes, methods, relationships and multiplicities.
title: The Issue Record Hub
answer: A class box has three parts: name / attributes (-) / methods (+).
Student: -studentId, -name | +borrowBook(), +returnBook(). Librarian: -staffId, -name | +issueBook(), +collectFine().
IssueRecord: -issueDate, -dueDate | +markReturned(), +isOverdue(). Book: -bookId, -title | +isAvailable(), +updateCopies(). Fine: -amount, -paid | +calculate(), +pay().
Associations (plain lines): Student borrows IssueRecord, Librarian creates IssueRecord, IssueRecord is for Book, IssueRecord gets Fine.
Multiplicities: Student 1 to 0..* IssueRecord; Librarian 1 to 0..* IssueRecord; Book 1 to 0..* IssueRecord; IssueRecord 1 to 0..1 Fine.
Memory trick: the IssueRecord is the hub of the wheel.

subject: se
question: Draw a Use Case Diagram for a Library Management System (search, issue, return, reserve books; librarian manages records; fines for overdue books). Identify actors and use cases, with at least one <<include>>.
title: Vending Machine Diagram
answer: Actors (stick figures, outside the system boundary): Student, Librarian.
Use cases (ovals inside the boundary): Search Book, Reserve Book, Issue Book, Return Book, Manage Records.
Student is linked to Search, Reserve, Issue, Return. Librarian is linked to Issue, Return, Manage Records.
Issue Book <<include>> Check Availability (dashed arrow from base to included use case).
Return Book <<include>> Calculate Fine (fine is zero if returned on time).
Memory trick: actors outside, ovals inside, include means always.

subject: se
question: Differentiate between a UML Class Diagram and a UML Sequence Diagram (purpose, elements, representation) with an example.
title: The Map and the Movie
answer: Purpose: class diagram = static structure (which classes exist and how they are related); sequence diagram = dynamic behaviour (messages between objects in time order).
Elements: class diagram = classes with attributes and methods, associations, multiplicities; sequence diagram = objects with lifelines, and messages.
Representation: class diagram = boxes joined by lines, no time; sequence diagram = lifelines and arrows, time flows top to bottom.
Example (library): class diagram Student 1 to 0..* IssueRecord; sequence diagram Student sends issueBook() to Librarian, Librarian hands the book back.
Memory trick: class is the map, sequence is the movie.

subject: se
question: What is the purpose of code review? Explain any four benefits of code reviews.
title: A Second Pair Of Eyes
answer: Purpose: to find defects and improve code quality early, before the code is tested or released (teammates read the author's code before it joins the main project).
Benefit 1: early bug detection. A bug found in review costs little; found by users it costs a lot.
Benefit 2: better code quality. Code stays clean, readable and follows the team's standards.
Benefit 3: knowledge sharing. Author learns from the reviewer, reviewer learns the code, so nobody is the only one who understands it.
Benefit 4: team ownership. The code belongs to the team, so anyone can maintain it or take it over.
Memory trick: bugs, quality, knowledge, ownership.

subject: se
question: What does multiplicity represent in a UML Class Diagram? Explain 1, 0..1, 1..* and 0..* with examples.
title: How Many Rules
answer: Multiplicity shows how many objects of one class can be linked to ONE object of the class at the other end of an association; it is written at the end of the association line.
1 = exactly one (a Book has exactly 1 Publisher).
0..1 = optional, at most one (a Student has 0..1 LibraryCard).
1..* = one or more, at least one (a Book has 1..* Authors).
0..* = zero or more, any number (a Student has 0..* IssueRecords).
Memory trick: the first number is the minimum, the second is the maximum.

subject: se
question: Differentiate between <<include>> and <<extend>> relationships in a Use Case Diagram, with example and notation.
title: Always Or Sometimes
answer: <<include>>: the base use case ALWAYS uses the included use case; it is mandatory and usually a shared step reused by many use cases.
Notation: dashed arrow labelled <<include>> drawn from the base use case to the included use case. Example: Issue Book <<include>> Check Availability.
<<extend>>: the extending use case adds extra behaviour to the base only under a condition; the base is complete without it (optional).
Notation: dashed arrow labelled <<extend>> drawn from the extending use case to the base use case. Example: Pay Fine <<extend>> Return Book (only if overdue).
Memory trick: include is always, extend is sometimes.

subject: se
question: Differentiate between association and aggregation in a UML Class Diagram with examples and notations.
title: Playlist Versus Songs
answer: Association: the basic link between two classes (one knows or uses the other); equals, neither owns the other. Notation: plain solid line with the relationship name and multiplicities.
Example: a Student borrows a Book (Student 0..1 --- 0..* Book).
Aggregation: a special association, a whole and its parts (has-a); the parts can exist without the whole. Notation: solid line with an empty (hollow) diamond at the whole's end.
Example: a Library has Books; if the library closes, the books still exist.
Memory trick: the diamond sits on the whole, and empty means the parts can leave.

subject: cd
question: For E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→(E)|id design a Syntax-Directed Definition to evaluate arithmetic expressions; demonstrate for 3+4*5.
title: Parse Tree Does Maths
answer: SDD = grammar + semantic rules; every symbol (E, T, F) carries one synthesized attribute val.
E → E1 + T : E.val = E1.val + T.val   |   E → T : E.val = T.val
T → T1 * F : T.val = T1.val × F.val   |   T → F : T.val = F.val
F → ( E ) : F.val = E.val   |   F → id : F.val = id.lexval
3+4*5: leaves F.val = 3, 4, 5 → T = 4*5 = 20 → E = 3+20 = 23. Values are computed bottom-up on the annotated parse tree (synthesized attributes, S-attributed).

subject: cd
question: Design the LL(1) parsing table for S→aBDh, B→cC, C→bC|ε, D→EF, E→g|ε, F→f|ε.
title: Junction Table
answer: FIRST: S{a} B{c} C{b,ε} D{g,f,ε} E{g,ε} F{f,ε}
FOLLOW: S{$} B{g,f,h} C{g,f,h} D{h} E{f,h} F{h}
Rule 1: A→α goes under every terminal in FIRST(α). Rule 2: if α can derive ε, it also goes under every terminal in FOLLOW(A).
Table: S/a: S→aBDh | B/c: B→cC | C/b: C→bC, C/g,f,h: C→ε | D/g,f,h: D→EF | E/g: E→g, E/f,h: E→ε | F/f: F→f, F/h: F→ε ($ column empty).
No cell has two entries, so the grammar is LL(1).

subject: cd
question: Explain bottom-up parsing with an example. Also discuss reduction in bottom-up parsing.
title: Parse From The Leaves
answer: Bottom-up parsing builds the parse tree from the leaves (input tokens) up to the start symbol.
Implemented with a stack and two main moves: SHIFT (push next input symbol) and REDUCE (replace a rule's right side on top of the stack by its left side); then ACCEPT.
Example, E→E+T|T, T→id, input id+id: shift id, reduce T→id, reduce E→T, shift +, shift id, reduce T→id, reduce E→E+T, accept (four reductions).
Reduction replaces the handle (right side of a rule on top of the stack) by its left side.
Each reduction is one step of a rightmost derivation run in reverse.

subject: cd
question: Eliminate left recursion from: S→A, A→Ad|Ae|aB|aC, B→bBC|f, C→CF|Cd|g|h, E→g|ε, F→f|ε. Rule: A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε.
title: Break The Endless Loop
answer: Rule: A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε.
S→A, B→bBC|f, E→g|ε, F→f|ε are not left-recursive: unchanged.
A→Ad|Ae|aB|aC (α = d, e; β = aB, aC) becomes A→aBA'|aCA' and A'→dA'|eA'|ε.
C→CF|Cd|g|h (α = F, d; β = g, h) becomes C→gC'|hC' and C'→FC'|dC'|ε.
Final grammar: S→A, A→aBA'|aCA', A'→dA'|eA'|ε, B→bBC|f, C→gC'|hC', C'→FC'|dC'|ε, E→g|ε, F→f|ε.

subject: cd
question: Remove left recursion: S→S+(E)|(E), E→E*(F)|(F), F→F(S)|id.
title: Rewrite The Loop Away
answer: Left recursion A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε.
S→S+(E)|(E) (α = +(E), β = (E)) becomes S→(E)S' and S'→+(E)S'|ε.
E→E*(F)|(F) (α = *(F), β = (F)) becomes E→(F)E' and E'→*(F)E'|ε.
F→F(S)|id (α = (S), β = id) becomes F→idF' and F'→(S)F'|ε.
Same language, no left recursion: the top-down parser no longer loops.

subject: cd
question: Compute FIRST and FOLLOW for S→Aba|bCA, A→cBCD|ε, B→CdA|ad, C→eC|ε, D→bSf|a.
title: Who Stands Where
answer: FIRST(S) = {b, c}   FIRST(A) = {c, ε}   FIRST(B) = {a, d, e}   FIRST(C) = {e, ε}   FIRST(D) = {a, b}
FOLLOW rules: $ in FOLLOW(start); A→αBβ adds FIRST(β)−{ε}; if β is empty or nullable, add FOLLOW(A).
FOLLOW(S) = {f, $}   FOLLOW(B) = {a, b, e}   FOLLOW(A) = {a, b, e, f, $}   FOLLOW(D) = {a, b, e, f, $}
FOLLOW(C) = {a, b, c, d, f, $}   (C is before A, D and d)

subject: cd
question: Construct the sets of LR(0) items and LR(1) items for E→BB, B→bB, B→c.
title: Seven Grows To Ten
answer: Augment the grammar: E' → E (new start rule).
LR(0) item sets: I0 = {E'→•E, E→•BB, B→•bB, B→•c}; I1 = {E'→E•}; I2 = {E→B•B, B→•bB, B→•c}; I3 = {B→b•B, B→•bB, B→•c}; I4 = {B→c•}; I5 = {E→BB•}; I6 = {B→bB•}.
Transitions: I0 -E→ I1, -B→ I2, -b→ I3, -c→ I4; I2 -B→ I5, -b→ I3, -c→ I4; I3 -B→ I6, -b→ I3, -c→ I4. That is 7 LR(0) sets.
I5 = {E→BB•,$}; I6 = {B→b•B,$; B→•bB,$; B→•c,$}; I7 = {B→c•,$}; I8 = {B→bB•,b/c}; I9 = {B→bB•,$}. That is 10 LR(1) sets: the cores of I3, I4, I6 each split by lookahead (b/c vs $).

subject: cd
question: Define annotated parse tree with example.
title: Parse Tree Name Tags
answer: Annotated (decorated) parse tree: a parse tree that shows the attribute values at every node.
Grammar: E→E+T | T, T→T*F | F, F→digit; every symbol carries an attribute val.
Semantic rules: E.val = E1.val + T.val; E.val = T.val; T.val = T1.val × F.val; T.val = F.val; F.val = digit.lexval.
Example 3*5+4: digits 3, 5, 4 → F.val = 3, 5, 4 → T.val = 3×5 = 15 → T.val = 4 → E.val = 15 + 4 = 19.
Values flow from children to parent: these are synthesized attributes.

subject: cd
question: Why is LR parsing good and attractive? Also explain its demerits.
title: Powerful But Heavy
answer: Merit: handles virtually all programming-language constructs for which a context-free grammar can be written.
Merit: the most general non-backtracking shift-reduce method, yet as efficient as the others.
Merit: LR grammars are a proper superset of LL (predictive) grammars, so LR is more powerful.
Merit: detects a syntax error as early as possible in a left-to-right scan.

Demerits: too much work to build the tables by hand (needs a parser generator such as YACC); canonical LR(1) tables are very large; ambiguous grammars cause shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflicts and must be rewritten.

subject: cd
question: Explain viable prefixes.
title: Never Past The Handle
answer: Viable prefix: a prefix of a right-sentential form that does not extend past the right end of its handle.
Handle: the right side of a production that the parser replaces (reduces) at that step.
Example: E→E+T | T, T→id. The right-sentential form T+id has handle T. Viable prefixes: ε, T. Not viable: T+, T+id.
Importance: the stack of a shift-reduce (LR) parser always holds a viable prefix; when it does not, an error is reported.
The DFA built from LR(0) items recognises exactly the viable prefixes.

subject: cd
question: Discuss how YACC can be used to generate a parser.
title: The Parser Printer
answer: YACC (Yet Another Compiler-Compiler) turns a grammar specification into a parser written in C.
Specification file calc.y has 3 parts separated by %%: declarations (%token, C headers), translation rules (grammar + C actions in { }), supporting C routines (main, yyerror...).
In actions: $$ = value of the left side, $1, $2, $3 = values of the right-side symbols, e.g. expr : expr '+' term { $$ = $1 + $3; }.
yacc calc.y produces y.tab.c (LALR parser, function yyparse()); lex calc.l produces lex.yy.c (yylex() returns the tokens).
cc y.tab.c lex.yy.c gives the parser program; yyparse() calls yylex() for tokens, shifts/reduces using the tables and runs the actions at each reduce.

subject: cd
question: Discuss the applications of syntax-directed translation.
title: One Rule Many Results
answer: Syntax-directed translation attaches semantic rules (actions) to grammar productions; they run when the parser uses the production.
Evaluation of expressions (desk calculator): E.val = E1.val + T.val, so 3 + 4 gives 7.
Construction of syntax trees: create an operator node with the operands as children.
Intermediate code generation: emit three-address code, e.g. t1 = 3 + 4.
Type checking: int + int gives int; int + string is a type error.
Translation between notations, e.g. infix to postfix: 3 + 4 becomes 3 4 +.

subject: oop
question: What is the purpose of the package keyword in Java?
title: Package = Folder
answer: A package groups related classes and interfaces into one named namespace.
It prevents name conflicts: shop.Student and school.Student can coexist.
It controls access (default / package-private visibility) and makes classes easy to find and reuse.
It must be the first statement in the source file: package shop;

subject: oop
question: Which access specifier allows a class member to be accessed only within its own class?
title: The Diary Lock
answer: The answer is the private access specifier.
A private member is accessible only within its own class.
No other class can use it, not even a subclass; outsiders must go through public methods.
Order of openness: public > protected > default > private.

subject: oop
question: Can an interface contain a constructor? Justify.
title: Interfaces Have No Constructor
answer: No, an interface cannot contain a constructor.
A constructor initialises the instance variables of an object when it is created.
An interface cannot be instantiated, so there is no object to construct.
An interface has no instance variables, only public static final constants, so nothing to initialise.
The implementing class provides its own constructor.

subject: oop
question: What is the use of the finally block in exception handling?
title: Finally Always Runs
answer: The finally block contains code that executes whether or not an exception occurs.
It runs after try and catch, even if the try block has a return.
Used to release resources: close files, database connections, streams.
Only exception: the JVM terminates first (e.g. System.exit()).

subject: oop
question: Name the method used to start the execution of a thread.
title: Run Is Not Start
answer: The start() method of the Thread class begins execution of a thread.
start() makes the JVM create a new path of execution and then call run().
Calling run() directly is just a normal method call in the same thread (no new thread).
run() holds the work; start() launches it.

subject: oop
question: What is the significance of a protected variable?
title: Protected = Family
answer: A protected variable is accessible within its own class and within other classes of the same package.
It is also accessible in subclasses, even when they are in a different package.
Its significance is inheritance: a parent shares data with its children.
It is not public, so the rest of the world cannot touch it.

subject: oop
question: Name the default package imported in every Java program.
title: java.lang Is Free
answer: java.lang is the package imported by default in every Java program.
No import statement is needed for it.
It contains the core classes: String, Math, System, Object, Integer, Thread.
That is why System.out.println works without an import; other packages like java.util need one.

subject: oop
question: Should a class be declared abstract if it does not define every method inherited from an interface?
title: Unfinished Means Abstract
answer: Yes. A class that does not implement all the methods of an interface must be declared abstract.
Otherwise the compiler reports an error.
An abstract class cannot be instantiated.
A concrete subclass must implement the missing methods.

subject: oop
question: Difference between throw and throws.
title: Throw vs Throws
answer: throw is a statement used inside a method body to explicitly raise one exception object (throw new Exception()).
throws is a clause in the method signature that declares the exceptions the method may pass to its caller.
throw actually raises the exception; throws only warns, raising nothing itself.
throw takes one exception object; throws can list several, separated by commas.

subject: oop
question: What happens to a thread when sleep() is called on it?
title: Sleep: A Locked Nap
answer: sleep() pauses the currently executing thread for the given number of milliseconds.
The thread moves to the TIMED_WAITING state and uses no CPU.
It does not release any locks it holds.
When the time is over it returns to the RUNNABLE state and waits for the scheduler to give it the CPU.
If interrupted while sleeping, it throws InterruptedException.

subject: oop
question: Explain how to create a user-defined package in Java and import it into another program.
title: Pack It, Place It, Pull It
answer: Create: first line of the file is package mypack; then write the (public) class.
Save the file inside a folder named mypack (folder name = package name).
Compile with javac -d . A.java so Java builds the mypack/A.class folder structure.
Import in the other program: import mypack.A; (or import mypack.*;)
Class and members must be public; then create an object and call its method: A obj = new A(); obj.show();

subject: oop
question: Write a Java program demonstrating a class implementing two interfaces.
title: One Class, Two Certificates
answer: interface Flyer { void fly(); }  interface Swimmer { void swim(); }  (declarations only, no body)
class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer  (names separated by a comma)
Duck must define BOTH methods and make them public: public void fly() {...}  public void swim() {...}
main: Duck d = new Duck(); d.fly(); d.swim();
Output: Duck flies / Duck swims. One object answers to both interfaces.

subject: oop
question: Explain try, catch and multiple catch blocks with an example.
title: The Rope and the Net
answer: Exception: a problem at run time (e.g. division by zero); unhandled, it crashes the program.
try: the block that holds the risky code.
catch: the block that handles one type of exception; it runs only if that exception occurs inside try.

Multiple catch: one try followed by several catch blocks, one per exception type; Java checks them top to bottom and runs only the FIRST match. Put specific exceptions first and the general Exception last.

Example: try { int n = Integer.parseInt("abc"); int r = 10/0; } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("divide by zero"); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("not a number"); }  Output: not a number.

subject: oop
question: Write a Java program with a user-defined exception thrown when age is less than 18.
title: Throw It, Catch It
answer: User-defined exception class: class AgeException extends Exception { AgeException(String msg) { super(msg); } }
Method that checks: static void check(int age) throws AgeException { if (age < 18) throw new AgeException("Too young"); }
throw (no s) actually throws the exception object; throws (with s) in the method heading warns the caller.
main: try { check(15); } catch (AgeException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); }
Output: Too young (15 is below 18, so check throws and main catches).

subject: oop
question: Create a thread by extending Thread; state one difference between extending Thread and implementing Runnable.
title: Start Hires, Run Works
answer: A thread is a separate path of execution that runs alongside other threads.
class MyThread extends Thread { public void run() { System.out.println("Thread running"); } }  (run() holds the thread's work)
main: MyThread t = new MyThread(); t.start();  start() creates the new thread, which then calls run(); calling run() directly makes no new thread.
Difference: Java allows only one parent class, so extending Thread uses it up and the class cannot extend anything else.
Implementing Runnable leaves the single inheritance slot free (the class can still extend another class).

subject: oop
question: Discuss the access privileges of class members within the same and different packages.
title: Four Doors of Access
answer: private: accessible only inside the same class.
default (no keyword): accessible within the same package only.
protected: same package, plus subclasses in other packages.
public: accessible from everywhere (any class, any package).
Same class: all four allowed. Same package: all except private. Different package subclass: protected and public. Different package, unrelated class: public only.

subject: oop
question: Write a program showing one interface extending another.
title: Interface Extends Interface
answer: interface Animal { void eat(); }  (base interface)
interface Pet extends Animal { void play(); }  (an interface extends an interface using the keyword extends, not implements; Pet now has eat() and play())
class Dog implements Pet { public void eat() {...} public void play() {...} }  (the class must implement every method in the whole chain, and keep them public)
main: Dog d = new Dog(); d.eat(); d.play();
Output: Dog eats / Dog plays

subject: oop
question: Checked vs unchecked exceptions in Java with examples.
title: Gate Scan or Mid-Flight
answer: Exception hierarchy: Throwable > Exception > RuntimeException.

Checked exceptions: checked by the compiler at compile time; the code will not compile unless you handle them (try-catch) or declare them (throws). Usually external problems. Examples: IOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLException.
Unchecked exceptions: subclasses of RuntimeException; NOT checked at compile time, so handling is optional; the problem appears at run time; usually programming bugs.
Examples: ArithmeticException (int x = 5/0;), NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Key difference: checked = compiler forces you to handle or declare; unchecked = compiler stays silent and it crashes at run time.

subject: oop
question: Purpose of currentThread() in multithreading, with a small program.
title: Who Am I, Thread?
answer: Thread.currentThread() is a static method of the Thread class.
It returns a reference to the thread that is currently executing that line of code.
Use it to get or set that thread's name and priority; it is most useful when many threads share the same code, to know which one is running.

Program: main prints Thread.currentThread().getName() -> main; class Worker extends Thread { public void run() { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()); } } started with new Worker().start() prints Thread-0.
Output: main, Thread-0 (same code, different thread, different name).

subject: im
question: What are concurrent activities?
title: Same Time, No Waiting
answer: Concurrent activities are activities that can be performed simultaneously (at the same time).
They do not depend on each other, so neither waits for the other.
In a network diagram they start from the same event and run along parallel paths, meeting again at a later event.
Doing them together shortens the project; the longest path decides the project duration.
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. What are concurrent activities? [pause] Let's start from zero. A project is one big job made of many small jobs, and each small job is called an activity. Think of building a house. Dig the foundation. Order the bricks. Paint the walls. Each one is an activity. [pause] Now, some activities depend on each other. You cannot build the walls before the foundation is dug. But look at these two: digging the foundation, and ordering the bricks. Does the order need the digging to finish first? No. So the crew can dig while the office orders bricks, at the SAME time. [pause] So the question wants three things. What concurrent means. How it looks in a network. And why it matters. [pause] First, the meaning. Concurrent activities are activities that can be carried out at the same time, because neither one depends on the other. They run side by side, in parallel. [pause] So: concurrent means same time, no dependency. [pause] Second, the network diagram. They start from the same event, and run along parallel paths, then meet again at a later event. Think of a river that splits into two streams, then joins again. [pause] Third, why it matters. Because they overlap, they save time. The project does not take the sum of both. It takes only as long as the longest path. If digging takes ten days and ordering takes four, you wait just ten. [pause] So in your exam, write this. Concurrent activities are activities that can be performed simultaneously, because they do not depend on each other. In a network they run along parallel paths. Doing them together shortens the project, and the longest path decides the duration. And to remember: concurrent means same time, no waiting. Five marks. Secured.

subject: im
question: Why do we crash critical activities?
title: Crash The Critical
answer: Crashing = shortening an activity's time by adding resources (workers, machines, overtime) at extra cost.
Only critical activities lie on the longest path and decide the project duration, so only crashing them shortens the project.
Crashing a non-critical activity (which has float) saves no project time and wastes money.
Aim: meet a deadline, avoid delay penalty, earn an early bonus, cut overhead costs.
Crash the activity with the lowest cost slope first; stop when extra cost exceeds the saving.
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. Why do we crash critical activities? [pause] Let's start from zero. Every activity in a project takes some time, and the whole project takes as long as the longest chain of activities. That longest chain is called the critical path. Think of friends travelling to the same wedding, each by a different road. The wedding starts only when the LAST friend arrives. The slowest road decides everything. [pause] Activities on that slowest road are called critical activities. They have no spare time, no float. [pause] Now, crashing. Crashing means making an activity shorter by paying extra, for more workers, more machines, or overtime. [pause] So the question wants two things. What crashing is, and why we do it on critical activities only. [pause] Here is the reason. Suppose a non-critical activity has spare time. Speed it up, and the project does not finish one minute earlier. You only wasted money. But speed up a critical activity, and the whole project finishes sooner. Every day saved there is a day saved overall. [pause] So we crash critical activities to reduce the project duration. And why would we want that? To meet a deadline. To avoid a penalty for delay. To earn an early bonus. And to cut overhead costs, which run every single day. [pause] One more point. We crash the activity with the lowest extra cost per day first, and we stop when the extra cost becomes bigger than the saving. [pause] So in your exam, write this. Crashing shortens an activity's time by adding resources at extra cost. Only critical activities decide the project duration, so only crashing them shortens the project. The aim is to meet deadlines, avoid penalties and save overheads. And to remember: crash the critical, never the spare. Five marks. Secured.

question: What is the full form of GOLF? (inventory classification: Government, Ordinary, Local, Foreign)
title: GOLF: Distance Decides Stock
answer: GOLF = Government, Ordinary, Local, Foreign.
It classifies inventory by its source of supply.
G: items supplied or controlled by the government (government rules, slow).
O: ordinary items easily bought from the open market from many suppliers.
L: local items from nearby suppliers (quick delivery, small frequent orders).
F: foreign items, imported (long lead time, so order early and keep extra safety stock).

Cooking gas comes through a government-controlled supply. Rice and salt come from the open market. Vegetables come from the corner shop. And one special spice is imported from another country. [pause] Classification means sorting items into groups, so each group is handled the right way. Golf sorts items by where they come from, their source of supply. These items are supplied or controlled by the government, so orders follow government rules, and that is slow. [pause] O is for Ordinary. Standard items, easily bought from the open market, from many suppliers. [pause] L is for Local. Items bought from nearby suppliers. Delivery is quick, so we can order small amounts, often. question: What is JIT?
title: No Stock, Just On Time
answer: JIT (Just In Time): a system that produces and delivers goods only when needed and only in the quantity needed (right item, right amount, right time).
It works as a pull system: the customer's order pulls work backwards through the stages, signalled by kanban cards; nothing is made until the next stage asks.
Aim: near-zero inventory, less storage space, lower holding cost, removal of waste.
Needs suppliers who deliver on time, every time, because there is no stock to fall back on.
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. What is J I T? [pause] Let's start from zero. Picture a restaurant that cooks only when you order. No food waiting under the lights. Each plate is made as you ask, and it reaches your table fresh. Now picture the opposite, a restaurant that cooks five hundred plates in the morning and keeps them. Wasted food, wasted space, wasted money. [pause] A factory faces the same choice. Stock sitting in a warehouse costs money, takes space, and can get spoilt or outdated. [pause] So the question wants two things. What J I T stands for, and what the idea is. [pause] J I T stands for Just In Time. It is a system where materials arrive and products are made exactly when they are needed, and only in the quantity needed. Not earlier, not more. [pause] So: right item, right amount, right time. [pause] How does it work? It is a PULL system. The customer's order pulls the work backwards. The last stage asks the stage before it for parts, using a signal card called kanban, and that stage asks the one before it. Nothing is made until someone downstream asks. [pause] What do we gain? Inventory falls close to zero. Less storage space, lower holding cost, less waste. The price is trust. Suppliers must deliver on time, every time, because there is no stock to fall back on. [pause] In your exam, write this. J I T, Just In Time, is a system that produces and delivers goods only when needed, and only in the quantity needed. It works as a pull system, using kanban. Its aim is zero inventory and the removal of waste. And to remember: J I T means no stock, just on time. Five marks. Secured.

question: Define cost slope.
title: Rupees Per Day Saved
answer: Cost slope = increase in direct cost per unit decrease in time when an activity is crashed.
Formula: (crash cost - normal cost) / (normal time - crash time).
Unit: rupees (cost) per day.
Example: normal 10 days Rs 1000, crash 6 days Rs 1800: slope = 800 / 4 = Rs 200 per day.
The activity with the lowest slope is crashed first.
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. Define cost slope. [pause] Let's start from zero. Every activity in a project can be done at a normal pace, which is cheap. Or it can be rushed, which costs more. Think of getting to college. Walk, and it is free but slow. Take the bus, a little money. Take a taxi, and it is quick, but expensive. The more minutes you save, the more you pay. [pause] In a project, every activity has two points. The normal point, with normal time and normal cost. And the crash point, with the shortest possible time, and a higher crash cost. [pause] So the question wants one definition, and the formula that goes with it. [pause] Join those two points with a straight line. The steepness of that line is the cost slope. It tells you how much extra you pay to save ONE day. [pause] The formula is: cost slope equals crash cost minus normal cost, divided by normal time minus crash time. [pause] Let's try numbers. Normal time, ten days, normal cost, one thousand rupees. Crash time, six days, crash cost, eighteen hundred rupees. Extra cost is eight hundred. Days saved are four. Eight hundred divided by four. Two hundred rupees per day. [pause] And here is why it matters. When we must shorten a project, we crash the activity with the smallest slope first, because that is the cheapest day to buy. [pause] So in your exam, write this. Cost slope is the increase in direct cost per unit decrease in time, when an activity is crashed. Formula: crash cost minus normal cost, divided by normal time minus crash time. Unit: rupees per day. The lowest slope is crashed first. And to remember: slope is the extra rupees for each day saved. Five marks. Secured.

question: How can we determine the optimum duration of a project?
title: Find The Cheapest Finish
answer: Total project cost = direct cost + indirect cost.
Shortening (crashing) raises direct cost and lowers indirect cost (overheads charged per day).

Steps: draw the network and find the critical path; compute the cost slope of each activity; crash the critical activity with the lowest slope one day at a time (shorten both if two paths are critical); note direct, indirect and total cost after each step; stop when crashing costs more than it saves.
The duration at which total cost is minimum is the optimum duration (the lowest point of the total-cost curve).
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. How can we determine the optimum duration of a project? [pause] Let's start from zero. Duration means how long the whole project takes. Optimum means best, and here best means cheapest overall. Think of a wedding. Rush it, and you pay extra for rush orders and overtime. Drag it out, and you pay the hall rent for every extra day. Somewhere in the middle is the cheapest. [pause] So the question wants the method that finds that cheapest duration. [pause] A project's cost has two parts. Direct cost is labour, material and machines. Shorten the project by crashing, and direct cost goes UP. Indirect cost is overheads, supervision and rent. It is charged per day, so a shorter project pays less. Indirect cost goes down. [pause] Add the two together and you get total cost. It falls at first, touches a lowest point, then rises again. That lowest point is the optimum duration. [pause] Now the steps. One. Draw the network with normal times and find the critical path. Two. Work out the cost slope of every activity. Three. Crash the critical activity with the lowest slope, one day at a time. If two paths are critical, shorten both. Four. After each step, note the direct cost, the indirect cost, and the total. Five. Stop when crashing costs more than it saves. [pause] The duration with the lowest total cost is the optimum. [pause] So in your exam, write this. Total cost equals direct cost plus indirect cost. Crashing raises direct cost and lowers indirect cost. Crash critical activities in order of lowest cost slope, and record the total each time. The duration where total cost is least is the optimum duration. And to remember: crash while the saving beats the cost. Five marks. Secured.

question: What is the value of Total Float for critical activities?
title: Critical Means Zero Spare
answer: The total float of critical activities is ZERO.
Total float = latest start - earliest start (= latest finish - earliest finish).
Critical activities lie on the longest path, so earliest and latest times are equal: no spare time.
Any delay in a critical activity delays the whole project by the same amount.
Together the critical activities form the critical path.
voice: [warm, clear teacher, friendly and patient] Today's question. What is the value of total float for critical activities? [pause] Let's start from zero. Float means spare time. Think of catching a train. The train leaves at nine. The journey to the station takes thirty minutes. Leave at eight, and you have thirty minutes spare. That spare time is your float. Leave at eight thirty, and you have no spare time at all. Zero float. [pause] In a project, every activity has an earliest start time, and a latest start time, which is the last moment it can start without delaying the whole project. Total float is the gap between them. Total float equals latest start minus earliest start. Or latest finish minus earliest finish. [pause] So the question wants one number, and the reason behind it. [pause] Now think about critical activities. They sit on the longest path. The project cannot finish until they finish. So their earliest start and latest start are the same. The gap is nothing. Total float is ZERO. [pause] So: critical means zero float, no spare time. Any delay in a critical activity delays the whole project by the same amount. [pause] A quick check with numbers. Activity A has earliest start zero and latest start zero. Float, zero. Critical. Activity B has earliest start two and latest start five. Float, three days. Not critical. [pause] So in your exam, write this. The total float of critical activities is zero. Total float equals latest start minus earliest start. Critical activities have no spare time, so any delay in them delays the project. Together they form the critical path. And to remember: critical means zero spare. Five marks. Secured.

question: Define PPC (Production Planning and Control).
title: Plan The Work, Work The Plan
answer: PPC is the function of management that plans, directs and controls the flow of materials, machines and men so that the right product is made in the right quantity, at the right time, at minimum cost.
Planning: routing (path and machine order) and scheduling (start and end times).
Control: dispatching (release orders to the shop floor) and follow-up (actual vs plan, corrective action).
Memory: route it, schedule it, dispatch it, follow it up.

question: What is a BOM (Bill of Materials)?
title: BOM: The Recipe Card
answer: BOM (Bill of Materials): the complete list of raw materials, components and sub-assemblies, with the quantity of each, needed to make ONE unit of a product.
It is drawn as a product structure tree.
Level 0 = end item (finished product); Level 1 = sub-assemblies; Level 2 = raw parts.
Each branch carries a quantity (chair: 1 seat, 1 back; back: 3 slats, 4 screws).
It is the key input to MRP, which multiplies it by the quantity ordered to plan what to buy.

subject: im
question: What are the two most important costs in EPQ?
title: Setup Falls, Holding Climbs
answer: EPQ (Economic Production Quantity) = the batch size to make in one production run at minimum total cost.
Cost 1, setup cost: paid once per run (tool changes, settings, labour, trial pieces); setup cost per year falls as batch size rises.
Cost 2, holding cost: paid on stored stock (space, insurance, capital tied up, damage); rises as batch size rises.
Total cost = setup + holding (U-shaped curve); it is lowest where setup cost = holding cost, and that batch size is the EPQ.

question: Centralised vs Decentralised vs Hybrid purchasing.
title: Hub, Plants, or Both
answer: Centralised: one central department (head office) buys for all plants; pooled orders give bulk discounts, standardisation and tight control, but it is slow for urgent local needs.
Decentralised: each plant buys for itself; fast, fits local needs, plant manager is responsible; but small quantities mean no bulk discount, duplicated work and differing prices.
Hybrid: head office buys common, high-value items in bulk; plants buy small, urgent, local items themselves; it gives the discount AND the speed.

question: Why is updating of the project network required?
title: Your Network Needs GPS
answer: The network is drawn before work starts, using estimated durations.
Actual durations differ from estimates (delays, early finishes), so the plan goes out of date.
Delays and changes shift the critical path and the floats (e.g. C takes 8 days instead of 4: the bottom path becomes 11 days, longer than the top path of 9, so the project needs 11 days).
Updating = enter actual progress, delays and changes, then recalculate times, floats and the critical path; this gives the revised completion time.
It allows corrective action (add workers, crash the new critical activities) and control, and a true date for the client.

question: What are the types of purchase orders?
title: Four Kinds of Purchase Order
answer: A purchase order is the buyer's written order to a supplier (items, quantity, price, delivery); once accepted it is a binding contract.
Standard PO: one-time purchase, everything fixed (items, quantity, price, delivery date).
Planned PO: long-term agreement; items, quantities and schedule known in advance, exact deliveries released later.
Blanket PO: repeat buying from one supplier at a pre-agreed price, no fixed dates; release an order whenever needed.
Contract PO: only terms agreed (price, validity, payment, delivery conditions); items and quantities follow through separate orders.

subject: im
question: Difference between EOQ and EPQ.
title: Bought vs Baked Stock
answer: EOQ is for purchased items; EPQ is for manufactured (made in-house) items.
EOQ: the whole order arrives at once, stock jumps to Q then falls. EPQ: stock builds up gradually while production and use run together; peak stays below Q.
EOQ uses ordering cost + holding cost; EPQ uses setup cost + holding cost.
EOQ = square root of (2DS / H).
EPQ = square root of (2DS / (H x (1 - d/p))), where d = demand rate and p = production rate.

subject: im
question: EOQ numericals: formula EOQ = sqrt(2DS/H), a worked example and how to solve the class sums.
title: EOQ Sums, Fully Solved
answer: EOQ = square root of (2DS / H); D = yearly demand, S = cost of placing one order, H = holding cost per unit per year.
Example: D = 9,000, S = Rs 200, H = Rs 10. EOQ = sqrt(2 x 9,000 x 200 / 10) = sqrt(360,000) = 600 units.
Orders per year = D / EOQ = 9,000 / 600 = 15.
Ordering cost = 15 x 200 = Rs 3,000; holding cost = (600 / 2) x 10 = Rs 3,000; total cost = Rs 6,000 (ordering = holding at the EOQ).
Method: write D, S, H in yearly units (if H is a percentage, H = % x unit price); apply the formula; orders = D / EOQ; total cost = ordering + holding.

question: What is a membership function in fuzzy logic?
title: Dimmer, Not Switch
answer: Fuzzy logic allows partial truth: any degree between 0 and 1, not just true (1) or false (0)
A membership function mu_A(x) gives every element x of the universe X its degree of membership in the fuzzy set A
Written mu_A : X -> [0, 1]: 0 = not a member, 1 = full member, in between = partial member
Example, fuzzy set 'tall': 150 cm -> 0, 170 cm -> 0.5, 190 cm -> 1
Common shapes: triangular, trapezoidal, Gaussian

question: Explain the Minimax algorithm with an example.
title: Minimax: Max Versus Min
answer: Minimax: decision algorithm for two-player, zero-sum games; MAX tries to maximise the score, MIN tries to minimise it, assuming a perfect opponent
Build the game tree, give utility values to the leaves, then back the values up from the leaves to the root (depth-first)
MIN node takes the minimum of its children; MAX node takes the maximum of its children
Example: MIN nodes: min(3,12,8)=3, min(2,4,6)=2, min(14,5,2)=2; MAX root = max(3,2,2)=3
Best move = the first branch, guaranteed value 3
Time O(b^m), space O(bm)

question: What is Bayes' theorem?
title: Bayes: Update Your Belief
answer: Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B)
P(A) = prior, P(B|A) = likelihood, P(B) = evidence, P(A|B) = posterior (updated belief)
It updates the belief in hypothesis A when new evidence B arrives
Example: 1000 people, 10 sick; test catches 9 of 10 and flags 99 of 990 healthy; 108 positives, 9 truly sick; P(sick|positive) = 9/108, about 8%
Applications: spam filters, medical diagnosis, Naive Bayes classifier

subject: ai
question: Explain the hill climbing algorithm and discuss its limitations.
title: Hill Climbing In Fog
answer: Hill climbing: a greedy local search; start from an initial state, look at the neighbours and move to a better neighbour; repeat
Stop when no neighbour is better; only the current state is kept, so memory use is tiny
Algorithm: 1 start state, 2 evaluate neighbours, 3 move to the best neighbour if it is better and repeat, 4 stop if none is better
Limitation 1, local maximum: a peak higher than its neighbours but lower than the global maximum, search stops there
Limitation 2, plateau: a flat area where all neighbours have equal value, no uphill direction
Limitation 3, ridge: a narrow slanted path up; every single step looks downhill. Fixes: random restart, simulated annealing

question: What is a semantic network? Explain with an example.
title: Canary Inherits Flying
answer: A semantic network is a graph that represents knowledge: nodes are concepts/objects, labelled arcs (links) are relations between them
Common links: IS-A (type) and HAS / CAN (properties)
Example: canary IS-A bird, bird IS-A animal; animal has skin; bird has wings, can fly; canary is yellow, can sing
Inheritance: can a canary fly? follow the IS-A link up to bird, bird can fly, so yes; facts are never stored twice

question: Differentiate between A* and AO* algorithms.
title: A-star Path, AO-star Plan
answer: Graph: A* works on an OR graph; AO* works on an AND-OR graph
Solution: A* gives a single path from start to goal; AO* gives a solution graph (sub-problem tree containing every branch of each AND)
Cost: A* ranks nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n); in AO* the cost of an AND arc is the sum of its children's costs
Update: A* has no back-propagation of costs; AO* revises costs backwards up to the parents after expanding a node
Use: A* for pathfinding; AO* for problem decomposition. Both are optimal if h never over-estimates

question: What is a crisp set? Differentiate between fuzzy sets and crisp sets.
title: Crisp Step, Fuzzy Ramp
answer: Crisp set: a classical set in which each element either belongs or does not; membership is only 0 or 1 (sharp boundary)
Fuzzy set: allows partial membership, any value from 0 to 1 (gradual boundary)
Membership: crisp {0,1} vs fuzzy [0,1]
Boundary: crisp sharp vs fuzzy gradual
Logic: crisp = classical true/false, an element and its complement never overlap; fuzzy = element can belong partly to a set and partly to its opposite
Use: crisp for exact data; fuzzy for vague terms such as hot, tall, young

question: Explain Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP) and their applications in AI.
title: CSP: Fill It, Break No Rule
answer: A CSP is defined by three parts: variables X1..Xn (what must be decided), domains D1..Dn (the allowed values of each variable) and constraints C (rules on which value combinations are allowed)
A solution is a complete assignment: every variable gets a value from its domain and no constraint is violated
Example, map colouring: regions are the variables, {red, green, blue} is the domain, constraint = neighbouring regions must differ (A=red, B=green, C=blue, D=red)
Applications: scheduling, timetabling, Sudoku, resource allocation (rooms, machines)
Memory trick: V D C = Variables, Domains, Constraints

subject: ai
question: What is a plateau in hill climbing?
title: Plateau: Flat Means Blind
answer: Hill climbing: always move to the neighbouring state with a better evaluation value
Plateau = a flat area of the state-space landscape where all neighbouring states have the same evaluation value

Problem: no uphill move is visible, so the algorithm cannot choose a direction; it wanders randomly or stops (the real peak may lie just beyond the flat). One of three classic problems with local maximum and ridge
Fix 1: allow sideways moves, with a limit on how many
Fix 2: take a big random jump out of the flat area
Fix 3: random-restart hill climbing (start again from a new place, keep the best result). Memory trick: flat means blind

subject: ai
question: Explain Alpha-Beta Pruning and show how it improves Minimax.
title: Alpha-Beta: Skip the Useless
answer: Minimax: MAX picks the highest child value, MIN the lowest; every leaf is evaluated (example tree: MIN nodes 3, 2, 2, root = 3, all 9 leaves checked)
Alpha-beta pruning gives the same result as minimax but skips branches that cannot change it
Alpha = best value MAX is already guaranteed (starts at minus infinity); beta = best value MIN is already guaranteed (starts at plus infinity)

Prune a branch when alpha >= beta. Example: first MIN node gives 3, so alpha = 3; second MIN node sees 2 first, so beta <= 2 < alpha and its remaining leaves 4 and 6 are pruned; third node searched fully; answer still 3
Improvement: same best move with fewer nodes; with good move ordering it can search about twice as deep in the same time
Memory trick: alpha is MAX's floor, beta is MIN's ceiling

subject: ai
question: Explain the complete process of a fuzzy system with a block diagram.
title: Fuzzy: In, Think, Out
answer: Block diagram: crisp input -> fuzzifier -> inference engine (reads the rule base) -> defuzzifier -> crisp output
Fuzzification: turns the crisp input into degrees of membership (example: 30 degrees is warm 0.67 and hot 0.33)
Rule base: IF-THEN rules (IF warm THEN fan medium; IF hot THEN fan fast)
Inference: each rule fires only as strongly as its input is true (outputs clipped at 0.67 and 0.33) and the results are merged into one fuzzy shape
Defuzzification: converts the combined shape to one crisp value, e.g. the centroid (balance point, about 61, so the fan runs at 61%)
Memory trick: in (fuzzify), think (infer), out (defuzzify)

subject: ai
question: Explain Bayesian networks and their applications in AI.
title: Bayes Nets: Nodes, Arrows, Tables
answer: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of random variables that models uncertainty
Nodes = random variables; arrows = direct influence (no loops); each node has a conditional probability table P(node | parents)
Joint probability = product of each node's entry given its parents. Example: Burglary -> Alarm -> John calls: P(B, A, J) = P(B) x P(A|B) x P(J|A) = 0.01 x 0.9 x 0.8 = 0.0072
Applications: medical diagnosis, spam filtering, fault finding in machines, speech recognition
Memory trick: nodes, arrows, tables

subject: ai
question: Explain backtracking search and constraint propagation in CSP.
title: Backtracking Meets Propagation
answer: Backtracking search = depth-first search that assigns one variable at a time, checks the constraints, and undoes (backtracks) the last choice when a constraint is violated
Example (map colouring, D fixed to blue): A=red, B=green, C=blue then D clashes with C, so back up to B=blue, C=green, D=blue works

Constraint propagation = use the constraints to remove inconsistent values from the variables' domains before and during the search, e.g. arc consistency: every value needs a supporting partner in the neighbour's domain
Example: D={blue} and C touches D, so remove blue from C; then A=red leaves C={green} and B={blue}: solved with no backtracking
Combined: backtracking picks a value, propagation cleans the domains; an empty domain means back up at once
Memory trick: backtracking = try, check, undo; propagation = cross out first
